case_analysis.focal_point: Whether § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act requires a federal district court to stay an action (rather than dismiss it) when the court compels arbitration and a party requests a stay.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act § 3, 9 U.S.C. § 3 (stay of proceedings pending arbitration) (with related FAA provisions, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16, providing the broader statutory structure).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the FAA’s text in § 3 is mandatory—when a dispute is referable to arbitration and a party applies for a stay, the court 'shall' stay the action—so the district court lacked discretion to dismiss even if all claims are sent to arbitration; they also emphasize practical and jurisdictional consequences (e.g., preserving a federal forum to confirm/vacate awards without forcing a new action and avoiding procedural gamesmanship around appellate jurisdiction and post-award proceedings).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that dismissal is permissible (or at least not forbidden) when all claims are sent to arbitration, relying on circuit precedent that treats dismissal as a pragmatic alternative to a stay; they contend Petitioners effectively conceded below that dismissal was a proper exercise of discretion, and they resist reading § 3 to eliminate district-court discretion or to require retaining a case on the docket when nothing remains to litigate in court.
key_precedents: Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018)
Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp., 500 U.S. 20 (1991)
Forrest v. Spizzirri, 62 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2023) (opinion below, as reflected in the record excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: The best argument for Respondent would be that dismissal is a pragmatic equivalent of a stay when all claims are arbitrable, but § 3’s text answers it: on a party’s application the court “shall” stay, and we do not rewrite mandatory statutory remedies into discretionary alternatives. Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize that allowing dismissal would also distort Congress’s appellate-review design in § 16 by enabling immediate appeals via a “final decision,” something Green Tree recognized as a real jurisdictional consequence rather than a technicality. Justice Sotomayor’s point about preserving an orderly federal forum for post-award proceedings reinforces that a stay is the narrower, statute-faithful path without opining on whether dismissal might ever be proper absent a stay request. Given the straightforward textual command and the structural fit with § 16, my view remains that a stay is required when requested.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest plausible respondent argument is that “stay the trial of the action” could be read as permitting dismissal once all issues are sent to arbitration, but that reading cannot be squared with the statutory command that the court “shall” stay the action “until such arbitration has been had” when a party applies. Justice Roberts correctly emphasizes that allowing dismissal would also defeat Congress’s appellate-jurisdiction design in § 16 by converting what § 16(b)(1) makes nonappealable into an immediately appealable “final decision,” a point reinforced by Green Tree’s discussion of dismissals as final decisions. Even if some lower courts have treated dismissal as a case-management alternative, our role is to enforce the text as enacted, and nothing in § 3 authorizes substituting dismissal for the mandated stay. No colleague’s reliance on Moses H. Cone or Epic Systems changes the core textual analysis; they confirm the FAA’s mechanisms are to be applied as written.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that dismissal is a permissible case-management substitute because § 3 speaks of staying the “trial”—fails on the statute’s mandatory trigger: on a party’s application the court “shall … stay the trial of the action … until such arbitration has been had,” which presupposes the action remains pending rather than terminated. Chief Justice Roberts’ § 16 point materially strengthens the textual reading: allowing dismissal upon a stay request would let courts convert a nonappealable compel-and-stay order into an appealable final judgment, an end-run Green Tree recognizes as a real jurisdictional consequence. Justice Kagan’s structural observation also fits the FAA’s integrated remedial scheme, which contemplates post-award confirmation/vacatur in the same proceeding without forcing a new suit and inviting gamesmanship. Nothing in our precedents affirmatively authorizes dismissal over a timely § 3 stay request, and under a textualist approach we should enforce the specific procedural directive Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that dismissal is a permissible, efficiency-enhancing equivalent to a stay once all claims are sent to arbitration, but § 3’s command that the court “shall” stay the action “on application” leaves no discretion when a party timely requests that protection. Chief Justice Roberts’ point about § 16 is especially persuasive: allowing dismissal would let a court manufacture an immediately appealable final judgment and undermine Congress’s calibrated decision to generally bar interlocutory appeals from compel-and-stay orders, delaying arbitration and increasing costs. Green Tree confirms the appellate consequences of dismissal, which makes the respondent’s “no harm” framing untenable in practice, particularly for vulnerable litigants who may face added barriers to returning to court for confirmation or vacatur. I therefore remain with the petitioner: a stay is mandatory when requested, and that reading best aligns text, structure, and fair access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent move would be to say a stay is merely a procedural mechanism and that dismissal is an equivalent way to “enforce” arbitration when nothing remains for the court to do, but § 3 answers that directly: when a party applies, the court “shall” stay the action “until such arbitration has been had,” which is hard to square with discretion to end the case. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about § 16’s calibrated appellate scheme is especially persuasive—Green Tree confirms dismissal manufactures an immediately appealable final decision, effectively defeating § 16(b)(1)’s bar on interlocutory appeals from compel-and-stay orders. Justice Sotomayor’s practical concern dovetails with the statute’s design: a stay preserves the court’s continuing, limited role for post-award motions without forcing a new lawsuit and potential jurisdictional whiplash. Nothing in our precedents squarely authorizes dismissal over a requested § 3 stay, so the text-and-structure reading remains the best, most coherent fit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that dismissal is a pragmatic equivalent of a stay once all claims are sent to arbitration, but § 3 does not ask what is “equivalent”; it commands that the court “shall … stay” on a party’s application, and a dismissal is not a stay in ordinary legal usage. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about § 16 is also powerful: permitting dismissal when a stay is requested would let courts (or parties) manufacture an immediately appealable “final decision,” undermining Congress’s deliberate choice in § 16(b)(1) to withhold interlocutory appeals from compelled-arbitration orders accompanied by stays. Green Tree, as Justice Kagan notes, confirms that a dismissal changes the appellate posture—so reading § 3 to allow dismissal despite a stay request invites an end-run around the statutory scheme. Under a textualist and separation-of-powers approach, we enforce the statute Congress wrote, not a judge-made convenience rule, so my vote remains for Petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest counterargument is that dismissal can be an efficient “functional equivalent” of a stay when all claims are arbitrable, but the text of § 3 answers that: Congress said the court “shall” stay the action upon a party’s application, and we do not rewrite mandatory procedural directives for convenience. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about § 16 is especially persuasive institutionally and structurally—allowing dismissal when a stay is requested would let courts (and litigants) manufacture immediate appellate jurisdiction under § 16(a)(3), circumventing § 16(b)(1)’s calibrated bar and inviting delay and gamesmanship. Green Tree confirms dismissal changes the appeal posture, and no precedent squarely authorizes dismissal in the face of a timely § 3 stay request. A uniform mandatory-stay rule is faithful to the statute, preserves the FAA’s remedial scheme for post-award proceedings, and avoids needless jurisdictional maneuvering.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent move would be to treat § 3’s “stay the trial of the action” as leaving room to dismiss the action entirely once all claims are arbitrable, but that reading is hard to reconcile with the mandatory “shall … stay” triggered “on application of one of the parties” and with the statute’s contemplation of continued judicial involvement after arbitration (e.g., confirmation/vacatur). Chief Justice Roberts’ point about § 16 is particularly reinforcing: permitting dismissal over a requested stay would allow parties to manufacture an immediately appealable final decision under § 16(a)(3), circumventing § 16(b)(1)’s bar on interlocutory appeals—exactly the appellate-structure concern Green Tree identifies when dismissal occurs. Nothing in our precedent squarely authorizes overriding § 3’s command when a stay is requested, and circuit practice cannot supply discretion the text withholds. On an original public meaning reading, “stay” means pause, not terminate, so dismissal is inconsistent with the statutory instruction when a party timely applies.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is administrative efficiency: if every claim is headed to arbitration, dismissal looks like a practical substitute for a stay. But as the Chief Justice stresses, § 3 makes the stay mandatory “on application,” and under a procedural-fairness lens that matters because litigants—especially less resourced ones—are entitled to the statutory pathway Congress chose, not a judge-made shortcut that can add cost and jurisdictional friction. Justice Kagan’s § 16 structural point also sharpens the real-world consequences: dismissal converts a nonappealable order into an immediately appealable final decision, inviting delay and strategic behavior inconsistent with Congress’s calibrated review scheme that Green Tree merely recognizes rather than authorizes. No precedent cited by colleagues supplies authority to override a timely stay request, so my view remains that dismissal is impermissible when § 3 is invoked.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3 provides that when an issue is referable to arbitration, the court “shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action” pending arbitration, and that mandatory language leaves no discretion to dismiss once a stay is requested. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would also undermine Congress’s calibrated appellate-jurisdiction scheme in § 16, because a dismissal can create an immediately appealable “final decision” even though § 16(b)(1) generally bars interlocutory appeals from orders compelling arbitration and staying the case. Our precedents treat the FAA’s procedural directives as binding and emphasize enforcing arbitration “in accordance with the terms of the agreement,” see Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018), and Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79 (2000), confirms that dismissal materially changes the appellate posture. A narrow ruling requiring a stay when requested follows the statute’s text, respects precedent, and promotes uniformity and institutional legitimacy by removing a circuit split without broader pronouncements about dismissal in other settings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of FAA § 3 is mandatory: when a suit is “referable to arbitration” and a party applies, the court “shall … stay the trial of the action” until arbitration is completed, and nothing in the statute authorizes dismissal in lieu of the commanded stay. Reading “shall” in accordance with its ordinary meaning at enactment, and respecting Congress’ structural choice in FAA § 16(b)(1) to bar interlocutory appeals from orders compelling arbitration accompanied by a § 3 stay, a discretionary-dismissal rule would create an end-run around that design by converting the order into an immediately appealable “final decision.” See 9 U.S.C. §§ 3, 16; Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79, 86–89 (2000). Our cases enforcing the FAA as written confirm that courts must follow the statute’s terms rather than judicially craft pragmatic alternatives. See Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA provides that when an issue is referable to arbitration, the court “shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action” until arbitration is completed, 9 U.S.C. § 3, and that mandatory language leaves no room for a district court to dismiss when a party requests a stay. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would also undermine Congress’s appellate-jurisdiction scheme in § 16, because a dismissal can create an immediately appealable final decision under 9 U.S.C. § 16(a)(3), effectively allowing an end-run around § 16(b)(1)’s bar on appeals from orders compelling arbitration and staying the case, as recognized in Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79, 86–89 (2000). The FAA’s structure and our insistence that its terms be enforced as written, see Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, 138 S. Ct. 1612 (2018), confirm that the proper course on a timely application is a stay, not dismissal. Practical consequences reinforce that conclusion by preserving a single federal forum for post-arbitration proceedings without forcing a new action or incentivizing procedural gamesmanship.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA is written in mandatory terms: when a suit involves an issue “referable to arbitration” and a party applies for a stay, the court “shall” stay the action pending arbitration, leaving no discretion to dismiss in the face of a timely stay request. This reading follows the statute’s plain text and this Court’s recognition that § 3 is a “device for enforcing an arbitration agreement” designed to move parties out of court and into arbitration efficiently. See 9 U.S.C. § 3; Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 22 (1983). A mandatory stay also avoids unfair practical consequences—like enabling immediate appeals through dismissal under 9 U.S.C. § 16(a)(3) and forcing vulnerable parties to incur additional costs to refile post-award motions—while preserving access to court for confirmation or vacatur proceedings within the stayed case’s framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA provides that when an issue is “referable to arbitration” and a party applies for a stay, the court “shall” stay the action “until such arbitration has been had,” 9 U.S.C. § 3—mandatory language that leaves no discretion to dismiss over a stay request. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would also undermine the FAA’s structure, particularly § 16(b)(1)’s bar on immediate appeals from orders compelling arbitration and staying the case, by allowing a court to manufacture a final judgment appeal through dismissal. Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph explains why dismissal creates appealability, and the statutory scheme indicates Congress sought to prevent that end-run while arbitration proceeds. A stay is also the more workable, coherent course because it preserves the existing federal forum for post-award proceedings without requiring a new action, consistent with the FAA’s integrated remedial design (see also Badgerow v. Walters on the limits and structure of federal-court involvement in FAA enforcement).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3’s text is mandatory: when an issue is referable to arbitration and a party applies for a stay, the court "shall ... stay the trial of the action" until arbitration is had. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal despite a requested stay would disregard that plain command and would undermine Congress’s appellate-jurisdiction design in § 16, which bars immediate appeals from orders compelling arbitration and staying the case, while allowing appeals from final dismissals. Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph confirms that a dismissal coupled with compelled arbitration is a "final decision" appealable under § 16(a)(3), so allowing dismissal on request would create an end-run around § 16(b)(1). This Court’s FAA cases, including Epic Systems, reinforce that courts must enforce arbitration statutes and agreements according to their terms, and § 3’s terms require a stay when sought.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3 of the FAA provides that when claims are “referable to arbitration,” the court “shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action” pending arbitration, and the mandatory term “shall” leaves no discretion to dismiss when a stay is requested. The FAA’s structure reinforces that reading because § 16(b)(1) bars interlocutory appeals from orders compelling arbitration and staying the case, whereas allowing dismissal would create an end-run to immediate appeal under § 16(a)(3), as recognized in Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph. No Supreme Court precedent squarely authorizes dismissal in the face of a § 3 stay request, and respecting the statute’s text, history, and workability counsels a uniform mandatory-stay rule. A stay also preserves a federal forum for post-award proceedings consistent with the FAA’s remedial scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3’s text is mandatory: when an issue is “referable to arbitration” and a party applies for a stay, the court “shall … stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had,” leaving no room to dismiss over that request. Reading “stay” to permit dismissal would conflict with the FAA’s structure—especially § 16(b)(1), which withholds interlocutory appeals from orders compelling arbitration accompanied by a § 3 stay, and would allow an end-run via dismissal and immediate appeal under § 16(a)(3), as recognized in Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph. This Court’s recent descriptions of § 3 as providing for a stay of court proceedings pending arbitration confirm the ordinary reading of the statutory command. Circuit practice cannot override the statute’s plain meaning, and a requested stay preserves the court’s continuing role contemplated by the FAA in post-arbitration proceedings.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3’s text is mandatory: when a suit involves an arbitrable issue, the court “shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had,” 9 U.S.C. § 3, leaving no discretion to dismiss once a stay is requested. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would also undermine the FAA’s integrated procedural scheme for appellate review—stays are generally nonappealable under § 16(b)(1), while dismissals can produce a “final decision” appealable under § 16(a)(3), as recognized in Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph—inviting gamesmanship and delaying arbitration. The Court has emphasized that the FAA’s mechanisms are carefully cabined and jurisdictionally consequential (see Badgerow v. Walters), and requiring a stay better preserves orderly post-award proceedings (confirmation/vacatur) without forcing a new action. Because this is a straightforward textual command with practical fairness benefits, I would hold that a stay is required when requested.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act requires a federal district court to stay an action (rather than dismiss it) once the court orders the parties’ dispute to arbitration and a party requests a stay.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. § 3 (stay of proceedings pending arbitration), in the broader context of 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the FAA’s text in § 3 is mandatory—when a dispute is referable to arbitration and a party applies for a stay, the court 'shall' stay the action—so a district court lacks discretion to dismiss the case even if all claims will be arbitrated; keeping the case stayed also preserves a clear procedural path for later court involvement (e.g., confirmation/vacatur) and avoids practical and jurisdictional complications created by dismissal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that district courts have discretion to dismiss (at least where all claims are sent to arbitration), and that longstanding circuit precedent permits dismissal as a case-management tool; they also emphasize that petitioners effectively conceded below that dismissal was an appropriate exercise of discretion in this case and argue that nothing in recent Supreme Court decisions (including jurisdiction-focused cases) clearly abrogates Ninth Circuit precedent allowing dismissal rather than a stay.

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point—invoking inherent docket-management authority to dismiss when all claims are arbitrable—cannot displace § 3’s conditional mandate that the court “shall” stay the action once a party applies; a specific statutory command controls over general inherent powers. Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s structural point about § 16 and Green Tree reinforces the textual reading: permitting dismissal would allow parties to manufacture an immediately appealable final judgment, undermining Congress’s calibrated limits on interlocutory appeals. Justice Barrett’s observation about the FAA’s integrated post-arbitration mechanisms (§§ 9–11), together with Justice Kagan’s Badgerow-based caution about jurisdictional discipline, confirms that a stay best fits the statute’s contemplated judicial role without expanding it. My preferred disposition remains narrow: we hold only that when a stay is requested, § 3 requires a stay, leaving for another day whether dismissal is permissible absent such an application.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that dismissal is permissible as a matter of inherent docket-management once arbitration is compelled, but that cannot override Congress’s command in § 3 that the court “shall” stay the action when a party applies for a stay. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito correctly emphasize that reading § 3 to allow dismissal would also defeat Congress’s calibrated appellate scheme in § 16 by turning a nonappealable stay-and-compel order into an immediately appealable final judgment, as Green Tree recognizes. Justice Barrett’s point about the FAA’s integrated post-arbitration mechanisms (§§ 9–11) reinforces that the statute contemplates a stayed action as the procedural vehicle for later judicial involvement, not a judicially created dismissal practice. Under a strict textualist/originalist approach, the statutory text and structure control, and any contrary circuit practice is atextual.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The best argument for the respondent is a docket-management one: if all claims are arbitrable, dismissal is said to be more efficient and functionally equivalent to a stay. But § 3’s text forecloses that once a party requests a stay—the court “shall” stay—which, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, cannot be overridden by inherent authority. Chief Justice Roberts is also right that allowing dismissal would subvert Congress’s calibrated appellate scheme in § 16 by transforming a nonappealable stay-and-compel order into an immediately appealable final judgment under Green Tree, a practical consequence that strongly confirms the textual reading. No precedent cited by colleagues suggests we may rewrite § 3 for convenience, so my vote remains with petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent-facing point would be that dismissal is an efficient exercise of inherent docket-management power once all claims are sent to arbitration, but § 3 answers that: when a party applies, the court “shall” stay, and inherent authority cannot override Congress’s chosen procedure. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly emphasize how allowing dismissal would invite an end-run around § 16’s calibrated appeal scheme—turning a nonappealable stay-and-compel order into an immediately appealable “final decision” under Green Tree—creating delay and leverage that disproportionately burdens individual litigants. Justice Barrett’s reminder of Badgerow’s jurisdictional cautions reinforces that a stay best preserves a clear path for post-arbitration proceedings without creating avoidable jurisdictional and procedural traps. On pragmatic grounds, a mandatory stay protects access to justice by keeping the courthouse door meaningfully open for confirmation or vacatur without forcing parties to restart litigation or bankroll premature appeals.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—invoking inherent docket-management authority to dismiss once everything is sent to arbitration—runs into the statutory wall of § 3: when the court is satisfied the issue is arbitrable and a party applies, it “shall” stay, and inherent authority can’t displace a specific command. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point about § 16 and Green Tree is also a practical, coherence-forcing reason to reject dismissal: it would let parties convert an otherwise nonappealable stay-and-compel order into an immediately appealable “final decision,” defeating Congress’s calibrated appellate scheme. Justice Barrett’s Badgerow-inflected caution reinforces that we should not create extra jurisdictional/procedural detours by dismissing cases the statute says to hold in place for the FAA’s post-arbitration mechanisms. Efficiency concerns may be real, but under a pragmatic textualism the workable solution is to follow the enacted procedure—stay when requested—because it reduces gamesmanship and preserves the integrated statutory design.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The best argument for Respondent is that district courts possess inherent docket-management authority to dismiss when all claims are sent to arbitration, but that contention cannot overcome Congress’s explicit command in § 3: upon a party’s application the court “shall” stay the action. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito note, permitting dismissal would also allow an end-run around § 16’s calibrated appellate scheme by converting a nonappealable stay-and-compel order into an immediately appealable “final decision,” exactly the consequence Green Tree identifies. Nothing in our FAA cases cited by Respondent’s camp (e.g., general pro-arbitration language in Epic Systems or Gilmer) authorizes rewriting § 3’s procedural directive, and our separation-of-powers principles counsel against substituting judge-made efficiency for enacted text. Accordingly, the statute’s text and structure require a stay when requested, even if dismissal might seem administratively convenient.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best respondent-side argument is that district courts have traditional docket-management discretion to dismiss when all claims are sent to arbitration, but that inherent authority cannot override Congress’s explicit command in § 3 that the court “shall” stay the action when a party applies. For those reasons, I remain with petitioner.

Nothing in this Court’s FAA precedents has expressly approved dismissal in lieu of a requested stay, and adhering to the text and the Act’s workability best respects precedent and institutional stability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3 provides that when an issue is referable to arbitration, the court “shall on application of one of the parties stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been had,” 9 U.S.C. § 3; the mandatory “shall” coupled with the express condition (“on application”) leaves no textual room for dismissal once a stay is requested. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would effectively rewrite the statute’s remedial command and undermine the FAA’s integrated scheme for post-arbitration judicial action (e.g., confirmation or vacatur under §§ 9–11), a concern reinforced by our recent jurisdiction-focused FAA decisions like Badgerow v. Walters. Although some circuits have allowed dismissal as a case-management practice, that atextual exception cannot supersede the statute’s plain meaning, and precedent favoring enforcement of arbitration agreements (e.g., Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis; Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp.) does not authorize courts to disregard § 3’s procedural directive. Accordingly, when a party applies for a stay, the district court must stay the action rather than dismiss it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3’s text is mandatory: when an issue is referable to arbitration and a party applies, the court “shall … stay the trial of the action until” arbitration is completed, leaving no discretion to dismiss in the face of a stay request. Reading § 3 to permit dismissal would undermine the FAA’s structure—especially § 16’s calibrated appeal scheme—by converting an otherwise nonappealable interlocutory order compelling arbitration (and staying under § 3) into an immediately appealable “final decision” via dismissal, as recognized in Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph. That practical consequence would invite delay and gamesmanship and reduce procedural fairness by depriving parties of the orderly, court-supervised path for post-arbitration proceedings (confirmation/vacatur) contemplated by the FAA. Recent jurisdiction-focused FAA decisions like Badgerow v. Walters reinforce the need to respect Congress’s procedural choices rather than expand federal-court pathways through case-management shortcuts.
